title: Status page + customer comms templates by incident type (taxonomy v1)
creator: Talia Benson
project: Reliability Program: Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping
description:
## Summary
Create a small set of reusable, taxonomy-keyed communication templates for (1) Status Page updates and (2) customer email updates. Templates must be clear, consistent, and safe to use during live incidents—especially when root cause is unknown.

This work supports the Reliability Program’s goal to make incident_type an auditable field and to improve comms consistency across Hosted / Dedicated / Private tiers.

## Problem
Today, comms quality varies by incident commander and Support owner. We often over-speculate on root cause (“GPU issues”, “provider outage”) early, or provide overly generic updates that frustrate customers. We also lack consistent wording per incident type (e.g., “routing fallback misbehavior” vs “capacity shortage”), which makes it hard for CS to explain what’s happening without promising incorrect mitigations.

## Goals
- Provide incident-type keyed text blocks that can be used quickly in:
  - Status page: incident title + impact summary + updates + resolution
  - Email: initial notification + periodic update + resolution summary
- Keep language accurate when root cause is unknown; avoid over-specific technical claims.
- Make templates tier-aware:
  - Hosted: self-serve audience, minimal account-specific language
  - Dedicated: named cluster/capacity language, account team involvement
  - Private: connectivity/config framing, customer-managed environment sensitivity
- Provide a small set of “safe” customer actions (when applicable) that don’t imply fault.

## Non-goals
- Not defining the taxonomy (owned by SRE program work).
- Not creating a full design system component library; this is copy + structure.
- Not creating per-customer, contract-specific legal language (we’ll align with PM-912 but keep templates generally applicable).

## Audience / users
- Incident commander / SRE on-call drafting status updates
- Support/CS composing outbound emails and coordinating expectations
- Product/Eng leaders reviewing customer-facing comms for high-severity incidents

## Principles (copy constraints)
1) Describe observable symptoms + customer impact, not presumed causes.
2) Use consistent terms aligned to incident taxonomy (type/subtype) while staying customer-friendly.
3) Offer next update time when incident is ongoing.
4) Avoid “blame language” (customer misconfig, provider fault) unless confirmed and approved.
5) No promises on exact fix times; can state mitigation underway.
6) Mention workarounds only if they’re broadly safe and validated by on-call.

## Template structure (building blocks)
Each template is composed from these blocks (choose only what’s relevant):
- Title (status page)
- Impact summary (what customers experience)
- Scope (which regions / tiers / models) — optional; only if confirmed
- Current status (investigating / mitigating / monitoring)
- Customer actions (optional)
- Next update time
- Resolution + follow-up note

## Standard placeholders
Use consistent placeholders so incident-bot/Console can pre-fill later:
- {{tier}} = Hosted | Dedicated | Private
- {{incident_type}} and {{incident_subtype}} (internal) -> map to customer-friendly label
- {{start_time_utc}}
- {{regions_affected}} (if confirmed)
- {{api_surface}} (chat, embeddings, streaming, console/control plane)
- {{impact}} (elevated 5xx, increased latency, disconnects, failed policy updates, etc.)
- {{mitigation}} (traffic shift, rollback, capacity add, config change)
- {{next_update_time_utc}}
- {{support_contact}} (Dedicated/Private)

## Customer-friendly labels (mapping guidance)
Internal taxonomy should be stored, but customer text should prefer plain-language labels:
- Availability / 5xx / overload -> “elevated error rates” / “request failures”
- Latency regression -> “increased response times”
- Streaming disconnects -> “streaming interruptions / disconnects”
- Routing/fallback misbehavior -> “traffic routing issues” / “degraded failover behavior”
- Capacity/fleet shortage -> “capacity constraints causing throttling or delays”
- Control plane outage -> “issues updating settings / policies in the Console/API”
- Auth/RBAC failures -> “authentication/authorization errors”
- Telemetry blind spot -> generally avoid as a public incident type; communicate impact rather than monitoring gaps
- Private connectivity/config -> “connectivity issues between your environment and Redwood services” / “TLS/DNS connectivity errors”

---

# Templates

## 1) Status page — initial incident (generic)
**Title:** {{tier}}: Service disruption affecting {{api_surface}}

**Body:**
We are investigating an issue causing {{impact}} for some requests to {{api_surface}} {{regions_affected}}. Our team is actively working to mitigate impact.

Next update by {{next_update_time_utc}}.

## 2) Status page — update (generic)
**Update:**
We have identified the issue and are implementing mitigation steps ({{mitigation}}). Customers may continue to see {{impact}} intermittently while mitigation rolls out.

Next update by {{next_update_time_utc}}.

## 3) Status page — monitoring
**Update:**
Mitigation is in place and we are monitoring recovery. We are seeing improvement in {{impact}} and will continue to watch system behavior before declaring full resolution.

Next update by {{next_update_time_utc}}.

## 4) Status page — resolved
**Resolved:**
This incident has been resolved. {{api_surface}} is operating normally.

If you continue to see issues, please contact Support.

---

# Incident-type keyed snippets (drop-in blocks)
These are optional blocks to swap into the “Body” section above when the incident_type is known.

## A) Elevated error rates / request failures (Availability)
**Impact (safe):**
Some requests may fail with elevated 5xx errors or timeouts.

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are mitigating by reducing load, shifting traffic, and restoring healthy capacity.

**Customer actions (optional, safe):**
If possible, retry failed requests with exponential backoff.

## B) Latency regression
**Impact (safe):**
Some requests may succeed but take longer than normal to complete.

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are investigating performance degradation and rolling out mitigations to reduce response times.

**Customer actions (optional):**
If your application supports it, consider temporarily lowering concurrency or setting a shorter request timeout with retries.

## C) Streaming interruptions
**Impact (safe):**
Streaming responses may disconnect, stall, or terminate early for some requests.

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are investigating the streaming path and implementing mitigations to improve stream stability.

**Customer actions (optional):**
If feasible, implement reconnect + resume behavior and retry with backoff.

## D) Traffic routing issues / degraded failover behavior
**Impact (safe):**
Some requests may be routed in a way that increases failures or latency, especially during failover or high load.

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are correcting routing behavior and validating fallback paths to restore expected performance.

## E) Capacity constraints / throttling
**Impact (safe):**
Customers may see throttling (429s), queueing, timeouts, or elevated latency due to capacity constraints.

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are adding capacity and adjusting traffic management to reduce throttling and restore headroom.

**Customer actions (optional):**
If possible, reduce burst concurrency and ensure retries respect backoff to avoid compounding load.

## F) Control plane / Console settings update failures
**Impact (safe):**
Some customers may be unable to update configuration (e.g., routing policies) via the Console or API.

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are restoring control plane functionality and validating configuration propagation.

## G) Authentication / authorization errors
**Impact (safe):**
Some requests may fail due to authentication/authorization errors.

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are investigating identity and access components to restore normal authentication behavior.

**Customer actions (optional, only if confirmed):**
No action is required unless we share specific guidance. Avoid rotating credentials unless requested.

## H) Private deployment connectivity (DNS/TLS/network path)
**Impact (safe):**
Private deployments may experience connectivity issues between your environment and Redwood services (e.g., TLS handshake failures, DNS resolution errors, or connection timeouts).

**What we’re doing (safe):**
We are investigating connectivity and configuration paths and will coordinate with your team if environment-specific validation is needed.

**Customer actions (optional, private-specific):**
If you have recent network/DNS/TLS changes, please share timestamps and relevant logs with Support to accelerate diagnosis.

---

# Email templates (Support/CS)

## 1) Email — initial notification
**Subject:** {{tier}} service disruption affecting {{api_surface}}

Hi {{customer_name}},

We’re currently investigating an issue causing {{impact}} for {{api_surface}} {{regions_affected}}. Our team is actively working to mitigate impact.

We’ll provide the next update by {{next_update_time_utc}}. You can also follow updates on our status page: {{status_page_link}}.

If this is urgent for your workload, please reply to this email and include any request IDs or timestamps you can share.

Thanks,
Redwood Support

## 2) Email — ongoing update
**Subject:** Update: {{tier}} disruption affecting {{api_surface}}

Hi {{customer_name}},

We’ve made progress and are implementing mitigation steps ({{mitigation}}). You may continue to see {{impact}} intermittently while mitigation rolls out.

Next update by {{next_update_time_utc}}. Latest status page update: {{status_page_link}}.

Thanks,
Redwood Support

## 3) Email — resolved
**Subject:** Resolved: {{tier}} disruption affecting {{api_surface}}

Hi {{customer_name}},

This incident has been resolved and {{api_surface}} is operating normally. If you’re still seeing issues, please reply with any relevant request IDs/timestamps and we’ll investigate.

We will follow up with additional details as appropriate after internal review.

Thanks,
Redwood Support

---

# Dedicated tier addendum (drop-in paragraph)
Use this for Dedicated customers when appropriate:

“Your dedicated deployment {{dedicated_cluster_name}} may have been impacted. If you have a specific throughput/latency target you need us to prioritize during recovery, please reply and we’ll coordinate mitigation accordingly.”

# Private tier addendum (drop-in paragraph)
Use this for Private customers when appropriate:

“If you made any recent changes to your networking, DNS, certificates, or egress controls, sharing timestamps and relevant logs can help us narrow down the cause quickly. We can also schedule a joint troubleshooting session if needed.”

---

# “Avoid saying” list (common pitfalls)
- “Root cause was GPU failures / cloud provider outage / kernel bug” unless confirmed and approved.
- “Your configuration caused this” unless validated and reviewed with CS lead.
- “Everything is fixed” without a monitoring window.
- “No data was affected” unless Security Ops has confirmed.

# Review checklist
Before sending public/customer comms:
- Does language match an observable symptom?
- Is scope (region/model/tier) confirmed?
- Does it include a next update time?
- Any workaround suggested: validated by on-call + safe?
- For Dedicated/Private: did we include correct support contact path?

# Deliverables
- Copy deck (status page + email) with final templates
- One-page “choose template” guide keyed by taxonomy type
- Handoff to Docs (Elliot Price) for publishing in Support/CS playbook

# Open questions
- Should “Telemetry blind spot” ever appear externally, or only internally as an operational note? Current recommendation: do not use as status page title; communicate customer-facing impact only.
- For routing/fallback incidents: what wording is least alarming but still accurate for enterprise customers? (Need input from SRE + PM-912).
acceptance_criteria:
1) Templates cover: initial/update/monitoring/resolved for status page and email.
2) At least 8 taxonomy-aligned incident types have drop-in snippets.
3) Dedicated and Private addenda reviewed by tier stakeholders (Lauren Bishop, Vivek Kulkarni, Rachel Kim).
4) “Avoid saying” list and review checklist included.
5) Approved for pilot rollout with incident-bot + CS playbook (tracked in Confluence).
comments: 2026-01-10 — Rachel Kim: Strong preference for ‘symptom-first’ wording. For enterprise, include what’s impacted (API surface + region) only when confirmed; avoid model names unless customers are pinned to a model version contractually.

2026-01-14 — Dev Patel: Support needs a separate subject line variant for ‘control plane config write failures’ because customers interpret it as inference outage; propose ‘Console/API configuration updates failing’ phrasing.

2026-01-20 — Rafael Mendes: +1 on not externalizing ‘telemetry blind spot’. If customers aren’t impacted, it’s not a status incident; if they are impacted, describe the impact. Keep telemetry classification internal for reporting.

2026-01-26 — Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, call out that throttling can present as 429s and/or queue delays, but don’t suggest lowering spend/limits as the workaround. Prefer: ‘reduce burst concurrency temporarily’ if needed.

2026-02-03 — Vivek Kulkarni: Private connectivity template should explicitly say ‘between your environment and Redwood services’ (neutral) and ask for timestamps + error strings; do not ask customers to rotate certs unless we request it.

2026-02-07 — Elliot Price: Once copy is final, I’ll publish into the Support escalation playbook and add a quick “when to use which template” table. Please keep placeholders consistent with incident-bot fields.

2026-02-12 — Talia Benson: Action item—align wording for routing vs capacity with ownership doc so internal labels don’t leak into customer text. Will schedule 30 min review with Mina Haddad + Vanessa Ortiz.
next_steps:
- Incorporate Dedicated/Private stakeholder feedback into the drop-in addenda.
- Confirm customer-friendly label mapping with SRE taxonomy decision tree (keep internal types but present plain-language externally).
- Run a tabletop exercise: draft comms for one example from each of these types: overload/5xx, latency regression, streaming disconnect, control plane outage, private connectivity.
- Handoff final templates to Docs/Support playbook + ensure Status Page admins have the “avoid saying” checklist.
risks:
Risk of inconsistent language across tiers if templates are copied and modified ad hoc. Mitigation: keep templates short, add checklist, and link to canonical source.
Risk of over-sharing internal taxonomy terms publicly. Mitigation: use customer-friendly labels; keep internal incident_type visible only in ops views.
Risk of promising timelines. Mitigation: include “next update by” rather than “resolved by” phrasing.
